extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and patent firms involved in USPTO prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and filing Information Disclosure Statements (IDS) to the USPTO and complying with the duty of disclosure (37 CFR 1.56), including what to disclose, who has the duty, timing, materiality, consequences of non-disclosure, and strategic considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) refers to a submission of relevant background art or information to the USPTO by an applicant for a patent during the patent prosecution process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An IDS is the formal vehicle for bringing relevant background art or information to the examiner's attention during prosecution. It should identify and present the pertinent references or information the applicant believes are relevant to patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of Disclosure (37 CFR 1.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a duty on all patent applicants to disclose relevant art or background information that the applicant is aware of and that may be relevant to the patentability of the applicant's invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although there is no duty to perform a search of relevant art, persons associated with filing or prosecuting patent applications must disclose to the USPTO all known prior art or other information that may be 'material' in determining patentability. Treat this as an affirmative, continuing obligation while prosecution is ongoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who has the duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty falls upon: the inventors; the applicant or assignee; each patent firm/attorney/agent connected with the patent application; each individual associated with filing/prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that all listed categories of persons (inventors, applicant/assignee, counsel, and anyone involved in filing or prosecution) understand and fulfill the duty. The obligation is personal to those involved and is not limited to a single individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Information — What must be disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Information typically includes: other issued patents; published patent applications; scientific journal articles; books; magazine articles; any other published material relevant to the invention; office actions in related/foreign applications; litigation involving related patents; material from competitor analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose material irrespective of country or language of publication. Include foreign and domestic references, related-file-wrapper office actions, litigation citations, and any published material that could be relevant to patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is material if a reasonable examiner would consider it important in deciding whether to grant a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'reasonable examiner' perspective to assess materiality — i.e., would the reference have been considered important to examination. This is the operative standard for deciding whether to disclose particular items of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of non-disclosure / inequitable conduct (Therasense standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent applicant, with deceptive intent, fails to submit material prior art known to the applicant, then any resulting patent may be declared unenforceable because of inequitable conduct (Therasense v. Becton Dickinson, Fed. Cir. 2011).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therasense requires two elements for inequitable conduct: (1) Materiality — but-for materiality (the PTO would not have allowed the claim if it had known); and (2) Intent — the single most reasonable inference from the evidence must be intent to deceive. Non-disclosure with deceptive intent can render a patent unenforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to file IDS / timing and procedural consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of candor is an ongoing obligation: file initial IDS within 3 months of filing or before first office action; file supplemental IDS as new prior art is discovered; late-filed IDS may require fees and certifications; final fee can be paid only with allowable IDS submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with the specified timing windows: initial IDS within three months of filing or before the first office action, and submit supplements when new material is discovered. Be aware late submissions can trigger fees and require additional certifications; certain actions (e.g., paying final fee) have constraints tied to IDS status (final fee only with allowable IDS submissions).

rubrics_metrics.name: IDS strategic considerations and best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic points: cite art from related applications (PCT, foreign counterparts); cite art cited in litigation involving similar technology; avoid burying examiner with marginally relevant art (recent USPTO concerns); provide concise descriptions of foreign-language documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tips include: make sure to cite pertinent art from related/pct/foreign counterparts and litigation where applicable; do not overload the examiner with marginally relevant references (the USPTO has expressed concerns about 'burying' examiners); when disclosing foreign-language documents, provide concise descriptions to assist examination. Balance thoroughness with relevance to avoid negative perceptions or increased burdens.
